In a fictional discussion among three founders, either person could use one figure to think about where the business might be in three years. That illustrates their shared Intuition preference without implying that either will speak longer. The shared N means both look at connections and possibility when sourcing; it does not mean they are thinking about the same thing, and it does not mean a long conversation is automatically a meeting of minds.

The difference sits on three axes. E/I compares whether attention and energy turn more toward the outer or the inner world: one more often thinks things through inside a discussion, the other more often speaks only after the judgement has formed. Align the conditions first: the same draft, the same two hours, the same information, the same authority. In this fictional example, one line of inquiry tests the consistency of the draft if someone contributes more money or leaves. compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: the three passages below are editorial composites, used to show discussable trade-offs. They correspond to no real company or person and are not evidence about how either type negotiates. Equity registration, the validity of an agreement and tax treatment depend on the jurisdiction and the entity form, and specific arrangements should be checked with local professionals. The division of work follows who knows how, who is present and who handles outward contact, not type.

When two people negotiate equity together, friction tends to appear when one is revising clauses and the other is waiting for a clear word. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which part each believes must be handled first.

### Equity split: 60:40, fifty-fifty, or undecided for now

(Fictional scene.) Three people form a partnership, the capital contributions are 5:3:2, but day-to-day operations are run mainly by the one who contributed least.

One position is to set the split dynamically by contribution: give a base ratio by capital, then a four-year vesting period adjusted each year by actual input, writing "who is doing the work" into the mechanism. The other is to say the thing out loud first: what the operating partner actually wants may not be more shares but the certainty of "I decide this"; without confirming that, no adjustment of ratios will satisfy them.

Both readings can be right. Talking only about the mechanism easily produces something technically complete and emotionally failed; talking only about feelings easily produces several rounds without a number, with everyone guessing.

A workable approach has two stages: first let each person state in one sentence what matters most to them about this, without evaluation, and have one person record it as minutes; then move to numbers and confirm which points in the minutes need to become formal clauses. The minutes do not settle the allocation, but they give the clauses a shared basis for interpretation.

Negotiation review: before talking, each writes down two ratios — the lowest I can accept, and what I think the other deserves — plus one fallback, what I will do if we cannot agree. The three sheets are not exchanged; each keeps their own. Afterwards, go through them item by item: which expectations moved, why, and what remains unclear. A shift from expectation may come from new information or a deliberate concession, so this is a review, not a personality test.

### A couple's shop: whose name goes on the registration

Fictional setup: two people open a shop together, most of the money comes from one and most of the work from the other, and local registration rules allow only one name on the licence.

One sees this as a technical matter: it makes no difference whose name it is, the money is shared anyway, and a separate internal agreement can handle any split. The other cares about a different layer: whose name it is decides who is acknowledged in this venture, and if there is ever a serious argument, that name becomes a sentence — "this shop is mine".

This is not pettiness. The first trusts the relationship enough not to need paper; the second knows that even a strong relationship needs a version that can be stated in front of other people. A workable approach handles both at once: register according to the actual operating need and local requirements, and separately list what needs confirming — each person's contribution, operating authority, profit distribution, exit route — then decide which of those go into an agreement. Registration, equity ownership and the effect of an internal agreement are not the same thing, and how to arrange them should be checked with local professionals.

Counterexamples are common here: some ENTPs will say "put it in your name, I don't mind", and some INFJs will insist "put it in anyone's name, let's not damage the relationship over this". Type describes where the entry point is, not who is more generous.

The first misread is dividing them by "who argues better". INFJ can lay out an argument very clearly, and ENTP can be speechless when emotion rises. Expressive ability is trained, not a preference.

The second is dividing them by "who is more idealistic". ENTP will work on an idea for three years, and INFJ will refuse to move a cent on a quote. Idealism is not a word owned by one type.

The third is reading the difference as maturity. Calling ENTP "all talk" and INFJ "all feelings" turns a position in the model into a character defect. Both types can challenge an argument, hold to a principle, or give way for a relationship; such behaviour neither proves a process was engaged nor disproves a type.

The fourth is judging by the speed of speech, the thickness of the clauses, or who drafts first. Pace depends on experience and setting, the detail of the clauses on who has done similar deals, and the timing of a draft on how far this round has got.

Equity registration, the validity of an agreement and tax treatment depend on the jurisdiction and the entity form, and specific arrangements should be checked with local professionals. The division of work follows who knows how, who is present and who handles outward contact, not type.

When two people negotiate equity together, friction tends to appear when one is revising clauses and the other is waiting for a clear word. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which part each believes must be handled first.
### Equity split: 60:40, fifty-fifty, or undecided for now
(Fictional scene.) Three people form a partnership, the capital contributions are 5:3:2, but day-to-day operations are run mainly by the one who contributed least.

One position is to set the split dynamically by contribution: give a base ratio by capital, then a four-year vesting period adjusted each year by actual input, writing "who is doing the work" into the mechanism. The other is to say the thing out loud first: what the operating partner actually wants may not be more shares but the certainty of "I decide this"; without confirming that, no adjustment of ratios will satisfy them.

Both readings can be right. Talking only about the mechanism easily produces something technically complete and emotionally failed; talking only about feelings easily produces several rounds without a number, with everyone guessing.

A workable approach has two stages: first let each person state in one sentence what matters most to them about this, without evaluation, and have one person record it as minutes; then move to numbers and confirm which points in the minutes need to become formal clauses. The minutes do not settle the allocation, but they give the clauses a shared basis for interpretation.

Negotiation review: before talking, each writes down two ratios — the lowest I can accept, and what I think the other deserves — plus one fallback, what I will do if we cannot agree. The three sheets are not exchanged; each keeps their own. Afterwards, go through them item by item: which expectations moved, why, and what remains unclear. A shift from expectation may come from new information or a deliberate concession, so this is a review, not a personality test.

Fictional setup: two people open a shop together, most of the money comes from one and most of the work from the other, and local registration rules allow only one name on the licence.

One sees this as a technical matter: it makes no difference whose name it is, the money is shared anyway, and a separate internal agreement can handle any split. In the fictional equity discussion, one criterion is whether a rule can be applied consistently. Another is whether the agreement fairly recognises each person’s contribution. Either ENTP or INFJ could use both.

Both have to be counted. Only the first, and the agreement is cold; only the second, and the agreement is empty. faq_blocks.question: Negotiating an equity split, which item does each attend to more?

faq_blocks.answer:
Split "talking about money" and "talking about the relationship" into two separate times; do not run both in one conversation.

Agree on a fixed monthly reconciliation that covers numbers and plans only; if emotions rise, pause and continue the next day. The value of that rule is not efficiency but giving both people a time they can anticipate, so no argument erupts at dinner. How to set up accounts and split everyday expenses follows the couple's actual situation, and a property agreement can be checked with a local professional.

body: In a fictional discussion among three founders, either person could use one figure to think about where the business might be in three years. That illustrates their shared Intuition preference without implying that either will speak longer. The shared N means both look at connections and possibility when sourcing; it does not mean they are thinking about the same thing, and it does not mean a long conversation is automatically a meeting of minds.

The difference sits on three axes. E/I compares whether attention and energy turn more toward the outer or the inner world: one more often thinks things through inside a discussion, the other more often speaks only after the judgement has formed. T/F compares whether judgement weighs criteria that can be applied consistently, or people and values. J/P compares whether outer work forms an arrangement, or keeps a door open for new information. The three are independent and cannot be packed into "who is more rational, who considers people more".
### The same equity draft: what each may attend to

Align the conditions first: the same draft, the same two hours, the same information, the same authority. In this fictional example, one line of inquiry tests the consistency of the draft if someone contributes more money or leaves. Another asks how the terms recognise the person doing most of the work and affect the partners’ relationship. These illustrate different criteria that either type could apply.

Each focus has a cost. Watching only the structure easily produces something technically complete and emotionally failed: the founder's share keeps rising while they still feel like hired help. Watching only the people easily produces several rounds of conversation without a number, with everyone guessing what the others mean.

Who raises which kind of question at the table depends on who prepared the material, who handles outward communication, which round it is, and how much information is available. Someone with fundraising experience may ask about the human part from the start, and someone in a first partnership may open by asking for a term sheet; neither is a basis for typing.
### Why Ti and Fe are shared but reversed

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si and INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se. What is shared is exactly the judging pair, only inverted: ENTP's auxiliary is Ti and INFJ's auxiliary is Fe, and each one's third position is the other's auxiliary.

In this writing Ti means organising concepts and criteria in an internally consistent way, and Fe means taking shared values and the effect of a decision on people into account. A position is a description in the model; it does not predict who raises terms first or who responds to people first, and it does not say who is better at negotiating.

In the fictional negotiation, one person may consider it respectful to lay out the options, while another may want to hear each person’s concerns. Either can do both. The shared function names do not tell you which concerns someone has or whether they have expressed them.

The third position falls on Fe and Ti — ENTP's Fe and INFJ's Ti — and whether these are labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables. This page uses the common version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone speaks. Both base descriptions are the [ENTP profile](/en/personality/entp) and the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj).

| --- | --- | --- | --- |

body: Scope note: the three passages below are editorial composites, used to show discussable trade-offs. They correspond to no real company or person and are not evidence about how either type negotiates. Equity registration, the validity of an agreement and tax treatment depend on the jurisdiction and the entity form, and specific arrangements should be checked with local professionals. The division of work follows who knows how, who is present and who handles outward contact, not type.

When two people negotiate equity together, friction tends to appear when one is revising clauses and the other is waiting for a clear word. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which part each believes must be handled first.
### Equity split: 60:40, fifty-fifty, or undecided for now
(Fictional scene.) Three people form a partnership, the capital contributions are 5:3:2, but day-to-day operations are run mainly by the one who contributed least.

One position is to set the split dynamically by contribution: give a base ratio by capital, then a four-year vesting period adjusted each year by actual input, writing "who is doing the work" into the mechanism. The other is to say the thing out loud first: what the operating partner actually wants may not be more shares but the certainty of "I decide this"; without confirming that, no adjustment of ratios will satisfy them.

Both readings can be right. Talking only about the mechanism easily produces something technically complete and emotionally failed; talking only about feelings easily produces several rounds without a number, with everyone guessing.

A workable approach has two stages: first let each person state in one sentence what matters most to them about this, without evaluation, and have one person record it as minutes; then move to numbers and confirm which points in the minutes need to become formal clauses. The minutes do not settle the allocation, but they give the clauses a shared basis for interpretation.

Negotiation review: before talking, each writes down two ratios — the lowest I can accept, and what I think the other deserves — plus one fallback, what I will do if we cannot agree. The three sheets are not exchanged; each keeps their own. Afterwards, go through them item by item: which expectations moved, why, and what remains unclear. A shift from expectation may come from new information or a deliberate concession, so this is a review, not a personality test.
### A couple's shop: whose name goes on the registration
Fictional setup: two people open a shop together, most of the money comes from one and most of the work from the other, and local registration rules allow only one name on the licence.

One sees this as a technical matter: it makes no difference whose name it is, the money is shared anyway, and a separate internal agreement can handle any split. The other cares about a different layer: whose name it is decides who is acknowledged in this venture, and if there is ever a serious argument, that name becomes a sentence — "this shop is mine".

This is not pettiness. The first trusts the relationship enough not to need paper; the second knows that even a strong relationship needs a version that can be stated in front of other people. A workable approach handles both at once: register according to the actual operating need and local requirements, and separately list what needs confirming — each person's contribution, operating authority, profit distribution, exit route — then decide which of those go into an agreement. Registration, equity ownership and the effect of an internal agreement are not the same thing, and how to arrange them should be checked with local professionals.

Counterexamples are common here: some ENTPs will say "put it in your name, I don't mind", and some INFJs will insist "put it in anyone's name, let's not damage the relationship over this". Type describes where the entry point is, not who is more generous.

body: The first misread is dividing them by "who argues better". INFJ can lay out an argument very clearly, and ENTP can be speechless when emotion rises. Expressive ability is trained, not a preference.
The second is dividing them by "who is more idealistic". ENTP will work on an idea for three years, and INFJ will refuse to move a cent on a quote. Idealism is not a word owned by one type.

The third is reading the difference as maturity. Calling ENTP "all talk" and INFJ "all feelings" turns a position in the model into a character defect. Both types can challenge an argument, hold to a principle, or give way for a relationship; such behaviour neither proves a process was engaged nor disproves a type.

The fourth is judging by the speed of speech, the thickness of the clauses, or who drafts first. Pace depends on experience and setting, the detail of the clauses on who has done similar deals, and the timing of a draft on how far this round has got.

body: When two results disagree, check the assessment name, version, language and scoring convention first, then which situation you were referring to: a negotiation at work, or a disagreement in a close relationship. If the two labels are indeed ENTP and INFJ, the only shared letter is N; that means the two rounds agreed on the sourcing axis, and two rounds cannot confirm a preference stable across situations.

If the item bank reports dimension scores, look at whether E/I, T/F and J/P sit near the boundary, whether the same scale was used both times, and whether the situation referred to differed. These are factors that may affect interpretation; list them as items to check, and do not infer from the distribution of items that the item bank is faulty.

Put the practice in reviewable negotiation scenes: take two or three recent matters — how the work was divided, how a budget was set, who handled outward contact — and write three lines each: what you were weighing, how your role and the stage of the negotiation shaped the choice, and whether you would still weigh the same standard in another setting. The notes are for reflection; they are not scored and do not assign a type.

Each focus has a cost. Watching only the structure easily produces something technically complete and emotionally failed: the founder's share keeps rising while they still feel like hired help. Watching only the people easily produces several rounds of conversation without a number, with everyone guessing what the others mean.

Who raises which kind of question at the table depends on who prepared the material, who handles outward communication, which round it is, and how much information is available. Someone with fundraising experience may ask about the human part from the start, and someone in a first partnership may open by asking for a term sheet; neither is a basis for typing.

### Why Ti and Fe are shared but reversed

In the common four-function notation used here, ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si and INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se. What is shared is exactly the judging pair, only inverted: ENTP's auxiliary is Ti and INFJ's auxiliary is Fe, and each one's third position is the other's auxiliary.

In this writing Ti means organising concepts and criteria in an internally consistent way, and Fe means taking shared values and the effect of a decision on people into account. A position is a description in the model; it does not predict who raises terms first or who responds to people first, and it does not say who is better at negotiating.

In the fictional negotiation, one person may consider it respectful to lay out the options, while another may want to hear each person’s concerns. Either can do both. The shared function names do not tell you which concerns someone has or whether they have expressed them.

The third position falls on Fe and Ti — ENTP's Fe and INFJ's Ti — and whether these are labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables. This page uses the common version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early someone speaks. Both base descriptions are the [ENTP profile](/en/personality/entp) and the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj).

The six rows follow the same fictional startup scene, covering the first conversation, the follow-up and an exit discussion: the same draft, the same two hours, the same information and authority. If one leads the conversation and the other only observes, the difference in roles can explain what each person contributes; change the topic to something neither knows, and the difference is flattened by the lack of information.

Check the conditions first, then which basis is taken first more often; both types can use the other's approach, so the table is not for classification.

| The same event (one draft, two hours, the same information) | ENTP: the basis more likely attended to | INFJ: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The clause "split 5:3:2 by capital contribution" | Whether the rule still holds on a capital injection or an exit, and whether it contradicts later clauses | What this clause means to the person doing most of the work — whether it makes them feel like an employee | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| The atmosphere freezes mid-conversation | May make sense of the same ideas by talking them through with the group | May make sense of the same ideas by reflecting privately on what was said | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |
| Someone proposes "fifty-fifty now, adjust later" | Weigh whether the same standard for adjusting the split would apply to all founders | Weigh how the proposed adjustment would affect the founders and what each can accept | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| It feels like time to close | May keep several ways of writing the clause open until the shared concerns are clearer | May settle on a provisional draft clause and revise it when more information comes in | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| Someone raises a concern privately afterwards | May clarify the same concern through a conversation with the person who raised it | May clarify the same concern by reflecting privately on the feedback | Direction of attention, leaning E/I |
| Six months later someone wants out | Check whether the same agreed exit criteria apply consistently to a founder in those circumstances | Weigh how applying those criteria would affect the departing and remaining founders | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. Someone who handles contracts all year more often checks the clause structure first, and someone in a first partnership may only repeat "we get on well"; the same person also changes approach with duty, deadline and information, so these rows cannot be used to classify.

Scope note: the three passages below are editorial composites, used to show discussable trade-offs. They correspond to no real company or person and are not evidence about how either type negotiates. Equity registration, the validity of an agreement and tax treatment depend on the jurisdiction and the entity form, and specific arrangements should be checked with local professionals. The division of work follows who knows how, who is present and who handles outward contact, not type.

When two people negotiate equity together, friction tends to appear when one is revising clauses and the other is waiting for a clear word. This is rarely a matter of who is right, but of which part each believes must be handled first.

### Equity split: 60:40, fifty-fifty, or undecided for now

(Fictional scene.) Three people form a partnership, the capital contributions are 5:3:2, but day-to-day operations are run mainly by the one who contributed least.

One position is to set the split dynamically by contribution: give a base ratio by capital, then a four-year vesting period adjusted each year by actual input, writing "who is doing the work" into the mechanism. The other is to say the thing out loud first: what the operating partner actually wants may not be more shares but the certainty of "I decide this"; without confirming that, no adjustment of ratios will satisfy them.

Both readings can be right. Talking only about the mechanism easily produces something technically complete and emotionally failed; talking only about feelings easily produces several rounds without a number, with everyone guessing.

A workable approach has two stages: first let each person state in one sentence what matters most to them about this, without evaluation, and have one person record it as minutes; then move to numbers and confirm which points in the minutes need to become formal clauses. The minutes do not settle the allocation, but they give the clauses a shared basis for interpretation.

Negotiation review: before talking, each writes down two ratios — the lowest I can accept, and what I think the other deserves — plus one fallback, what I will do if we cannot agree. The three sheets are not exchanged; each keeps their own. Afterwards, go through them item by item: which expectations moved, why, and what remains unclear. A shift from expectation may come from new information or a deliberate concession, so this is a review, not a personality test.

### A couple's shop: whose name goes on the registration

Fictional setup: two people open a shop together, most of the money comes from one and most of the work from the other, and local registration rules allow only one name on the licence.

One sees this as a technical matter: it makes no difference whose name it is, the money is shared anyway, and a separate internal agreement can handle any split. The other cares about a different layer: whose name it is decides who is acknowledged in this venture, and if there is ever a serious argument, that name becomes a sentence — "this shop is mine".

This is not pettiness. The first trusts the relationship enough not to need paper; the second knows that even a strong relationship needs a version that can be stated in front of other people. A workable approach handles both at once: register according to the actual operating need and local requirements, and separately list what needs confirming — each person's contribution, operating authority, profit distribution, exit route — then decide which of those go into an agreement. Registration, equity ownership and the effect of an internal agreement are not the same thing, and how to arrange them should be checked with local professionals.

Counterexamples are common here: some ENTPs will say "put it in your name, I don't mind", and some INFJs will insist "put it in anyone's name, let's not damage the relationship over this". Type describes where the entry point is, not who is more generous.

sections.body_md:
The first misread is dividing them by "who argues better". INFJ can lay out an argument very clearly, and ENTP can be speechless when emotion rises. Expressive ability is trained, not a preference.

The second is dividing them by "who is more idealistic". ENTP will work on an idea for three years, and INFJ will refuse to move a cent on a quote. Idealism is not a word owned by one type.

The third is reading the difference as maturity. Calling ENTP "all talk" and INFJ "all feelings" turns a position in the model into a character defect. Both types can challenge an argument, hold to a principle, or give way for a relationship; such behaviour neither proves a process was engaged nor disproves a type.

The fourth is judging by the speed of speech, the thickness of the clauses, or who drafts first. Pace depends on experience and setting, the detail of the clauses on who has done similar deals, and the timing of a draft on how far this round has got.

When two results disagree, check the assessment name, version, language and scoring convention first, then which situation you were referring to: a negotiation at work, or a disagreement in a close relationship. If the two labels are indeed ENTP and INFJ, the only shared letter is N; that means the two rounds agreed on the sourcing axis, and two rounds cannot confirm a preference stable across situations.

If the item bank reports dimension scores, look at whether E/I, T/F and J/P sit near the boundary, whether the same scale was used both times, and whether the situation referred to differed. These are factors that may affect interpretation; list them as items to check, and do not infer from the distribution of items that the item bank is faulty.

Put the practice in reviewable negotiation scenes: take two or three recent matters — how the work was divided, how a budget was set, who handled outward contact — and write three lines each: what you were weighing, how your role and the stage of the negotiation shaped the choice, and whether you would still weigh the same standard in another setting. The notes are for reflection; they are not scored and do not assign a type.
sections.title: ENTP and INFJ: how to keep observing

items.answer:
They share Intuition (N), so the model describes both as drawn to patterns and possibilities. A single conversation cannot tell you how someone’s attention is directed, how they decide or how they approach commitments.

To separate them, look at the three axes rather than at what happened after the conversation. One more often cites "does this rule hold together", the other "what does this mean for the people involved"; outward, one more often keeps options and the other more often forms a statement. Whether five directions were listed afterwards or cut down to one depends on the information and the deadline, and cannot type anyone on its own.
items.question: Where are ENTP and INFJ most easily confused?

items.answer:
Because what is shared is the name of two judging processes, not the same set of concerns; shared processes do not tell you what either person expects.

The misunderstanding usually comes from unstated concerns: one has not said they need certainty in the mechanism, the other has not said they need to be acknowledged. Rather than guessing which process is at work, say both sentences out loud — "I need this rule to hold in every scenario", "I need to know my contribution has been counted".
items.question: Sharing Ti and Fe, why do ENTP and INFJ so easily misunderstand each other?

No. A single behaviour neither proves that a process was engaged nor disproves a type.

Both types can challenge an argument, hold to a principle, or concede for a relationship; that belongs to ability and choice, not to the boundary of a type. What discriminates better is which kind of basis is cited more often across comparable situations — whether the standard is consistent, or what it means for people — together with the role, deadline and amount of information at the time.
items.question: INFJ argues for argument's sake and ENTP talks about principles — are these counterexamples?

items.answer:
In the fictional equity discussion, one criterion is whether a rule can be applied consistently. Another is whether the agreement fairly recognises each person’s contribution. Either ENTP or INFJ could use both.

Both have to be counted. Only the first, and the agreement is cold; only the second, and the agreement is empty. A workable order is for each to work it out and then exchange conclusions, rather than calculating and arguing at the same table; who actually speaks first depends on who leads the conversation, which round it is, and how much material is available.
items.question: Negotiating an equity split, which item does each attend to more?

items.answer:
Split "talking about money" and "talking about the relationship" into two separate times; do not run both in one conversation.

Agree on a fixed monthly reconciliation that covers numbers and plans only; if emotions rise, pause and continue the next day. The value of that rule is not efficiency but giving both people a time they can anticipate, so no argument erupts at dinner. How to set up accounts and split everyday expenses follows the couple's actual situation, and a property agreement can be checked with a local professional.
items.question: As partners, how do they talk about money without damaging the relationship?

items.answer:
No single part can be kept as a stable conclusion; if the two labels are ENTP and INFJ, only N matches.

What can be checked is the scale version, whether dimensions sit near a boundary, and whether the two rounds referred to different situations; record these as hypotheses to be tested. Two matching results only mean those two rounds matched, and two differing results do not mean one is more "real"; talking about a stable preference needs more records under more consistent conditions.
